extracted.intended_audience: litigators, judges, legal counsel for news organizations and media-company executives concerned with news-piracy/unfair-competition
extracted.subtask_description: A legal brief arguing that a news organization (The Associated Press) has property and contractual rights in the news it collects and is entitled to an injunction against a rival (International News Service) for systematic appropriation of that news. Focus is on unfair competition, property-in-news doctrine, and injunction standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee prohibition on taking stories from non-members
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees should under no circumstances take for rewriting or republication any story of foreign or domestic origin from papers not members of The Associated Press or from papers conducting a news service of their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmative instruction to staff; evidence presented via affidavits (e.g., Harold Martin, Basil G. Wyrick) that employees were repeatedly instructed not to use or copy items from non-member papers and to verify any such items from other sources before use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized use of purchased/stand-purchased newspaper items
rubrics_metrics.description: The only authorized use of news items appearing in newspapers not represented by membership in The Associated Press was for the sole and only purpose of obtaining bare information that a certain event was said to have happened, whereupon the representatives of The Associated Press would undertake an independent investigation of the facts and write the story solely upon the strength of this independent investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under instructions, neither the details of a happening nor the bare statement of fact as appearing in such papers could be incorporated into AP dispatches; any use required independent verification and preparation based on other sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: By-law exclusivity for member-gathered local news
rubrics_metrics.description: All local news gathered by members for the complainant is to be received and used exclusively for publication in members' own newspapers; no member shall permit any other use or furnish such news to anyone who is not a member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By-laws and charter obligations make local news collected by members effectively the complainant's property for exclusive distribution among members; membership and by-laws distribute costs and restrict outside use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service-value dimensions for a news cooperative
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of the complainant to its members necessarily depends upon the adequacy, reliability, promptness, cheapness and exclusiveness of its service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five dimensions (adequacy, reliability, promptness, cheapness, exclusiveness) are presented as the evaluative criteria for the business value of a news-service organization and as the bases for injury when rival conduct diminishes them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited appropriation method — bribing employees to supply dispatches
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant bribed employees of a member newspaper (e.g., the Cleveland News) to furnish the complainant's news, as soon as received by wire, to the defendant's office to be at once transmitted over its own wires to clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as one of the defendant's principal unlawful methods; documented by specific letters and affidavits (e.g., Agnew, Gushing) describing secret arrangements and regular payments for immediate transmittal of AP dispatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited appropriation method — copying in editorial rooms / from receiving machines
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant obtained the complainant's news from editorial rooms (e.g., New York American) by entering those rooms and copying or extracting from the Morkrum receiving machine or the incoming copy as it was received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits (Eke, Koukol, Finnerty) describe employees of the defendant entering editorial rooms and removing copied AP material; characterized as a systematic and continuous practice used to appropriate foreign and other important dispatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited appropriation method — copying from early editions and bulletin boards
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant systematically and continuously copied the complainant's dispatches from early editions of newspapers published by complainant's members and from bulletin boards maintained by them, then transmitted the same to its clients as if gathered independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This third method is discussed at length with typical instances; defendant largely admits facts but disputes legal effect. Used to show how pirated dispatches were presented as defendant's own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal proposition: news as property (business commodity)
rubrics_metrics.description: News as a business commodity is property because it costs money and labor to produce and because it has value for which those who have it not are ready to pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the nature of news-value: novelty, accuracy, and presence where/when there are interested purchasers. The organization that converts events into a marketable message has property in that message (subject to limits discussed). Case law cited to establish the doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope/limit of property right in news
rubrics_metrics.description: Such an organization has the exclusive right to the property which it has itself created — i.e., its own message from the happening to those who seek to buy — but it does not have an exclusive monopoly to all announcement of the happening; other organizations may create their own messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that property attaches to the created message (the organization's product), not to the underlying event; other organizations may independently report the event but cannot appropriate another organization's created message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection by contract and relations of confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to property and unfair-competition protection, the complainant is protected by contracts and relations of confidence with respect to its news which it shares with its members and agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts, by-laws and relationships of confidence (e.g., member pledges) create additional legal bases to enjoin appropriation and to hold the defendant liable for inducing breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegality of surreptitious obtaining and inducement to breach
rubrics_metrics.description: Any attempt to show that the information obtained was used only as a 'tip' and not for publication is immaterial, since the mere obtaining was surreptitious and unlawful generally and was also an inducement to the breach of a contract and a relation of confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surreptitious procurement alone supports equitable relief because it both is unlawful and induces contractual/confidential breaches; AP adduces affidavits showing full appropriation, not merely tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction standard — any unlawful practice justifies relief
rubrics_metrics.description: This is an application for an injunction, and, if the proofs show an unlawful practice however slight on the part of the defendant, the complainant is entitled to have it stopped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes equitable remedy standard: even relatively small or infrequent unlawful acts, once proved, warrant injunctive relief; illustrates that a single leak can taint the entire service (one tapped wire sufficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial valuation elements of news
rubrics_metrics.description: News has value not in phraseology or tangibles but in its novelty, its accuracy and its presence in the place where there are people interested enough to pay, and at the time when they are so interested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify why news is a marketable commodity and why costs of gathering/transmitting news create a property interest; illustrates why appropriation undermines the economic model of a cooperative news service.
